                    Aegis: A Secure Programmable Exokernel
           Dawson R. Engler            M. Frans Kaashoek             James W. O'Toole Jr.
                              MIT Laboratory for Computer Science
                                  Cambridge, MA 02139, USA
                                             June 27 1994


                                                Abstract
          To provide high performance and a high degree of modularity, operating systems should
      provide only minimal embedded kernel functionality. The Exokernel is a new operating sys-
      tem structure that achieves this minimalist goal by letting applications manage the underlying
      hardware resources directly instead of hiding the hardware functionality in layers of operating
      system software. Applications can customize the operating system by extending exokernel in-
      terfaces. Exokernels can use code inspection, inlined cross-domain procedure calls, and secure
      languages to allow the safe execution of user code in the kernel. By having direct access to
      the physical hardware applications can implement policies that incorporate application-specific
      knowledge. To test and evaluate exokernels and their customization techniques a prototype
      exokernel system, Aegis, is being developed.

1 Introduction
An operating system is a virtual machine that abstracts physical resources. Existing operating
systems do more than encapsulate resources: they also implement policies, which control the use
of these resources. In addition, operating system implementors typically seize upon the hardware
supervisor mode to define the interface between applications and the virtual machine. The xed
resource policies and the supervisor barrier prevent applications from obtaining the full functionality
and performance of the hardware. In our view, the operating system should defer policy decisions
to applications and provide a secure programmable machine interface, so that applications have
direct access to the hardware and are able to set their own policies [15]. We are designing and
implementing Aegis, a prototype system that will test the feasibility of this approach.
    A monolithic operating system typically provides a single xed policy for resource manage-
ment. However, no single policy is best for all applications. For example, le system and relational
database applications often have different storage access patterns, and therefore benefit from dif-
ferent bu er and disk management policies. Similar policy con icts arise in almost every area of

                                                    1
resource management [2, 13, 19, 42]. While microkernels have pushed some policy decisions out of
the kernel into user-level processes, the supervisor mode still defines a xed interface among the ker-
nel, user-level services, and applications. Applications then su er from a large number of protection
domain crossings. These crossings are typically expensive, as they involve entering the supervisor
mode, saving and restoring registers, scheduling a thread of control, and manipulating address
spaces [3, 9, 38]. For example, many applications run slower on the microkernel implementation of
Mach than on the monolithic implementation [3].
     The disadvantages of xed operating system policies are made worse by the growing diversity
in hardware platforms and rapid advances of technology. For example, in a mobile computer
it is of crucial importance to save power by carefully managing the spin-down policy of the disk.
Using application-specific knowledge, spin-down policies can be much more effective than predictive
policies or static ones [13, 33]. New architectures are arriving that support protected user-level
communication, requiring little involvement of the operating system [8, 27]. By xing policies,
operating system software prevents applications from evolving with the hardware.
     In this paper we propose a new operating system organization, the exokernel, that delivers
hardware performance and hardware functionality directly to applications. An exokernel is a virtual
machine that lets applications manage their own physical resources (for example through the use of
libraries). By moving the management of resources out of the operating system kernel, an exokernel
allows for a high degree of customization. We see three reasons for customization:
    Tailor policies to given hardware con gurations, allowing applications to advance with the
     hardware.
    Tailor policies to given applications. For example, the interaction of application and the
     virtual memory system is crucial to the performance of applications. Closer integration with
     virtual memory management can enable distributed shared memory systems and garbage
     collectors to run an order of magnitude faster [4].
    Improve performance by reducing the overhead of interrupts, translation look-aside bu er
     (TLB) faults, traps, context switches, and cache misses, which are the primary sources of
     overhead in today's operating systems.
    By lowering the kernel interface to calls that match the physical hardware resources, we expect
the number of kernel crossings to be reduced, as most data structures and code will be living in the
application address space. To minimize the performance impact of crossing the kernel boundary
for privileged instructions and interrupts, and switching from one process to another process, the
exokernel allows applications to run user code safely in the kernel. In this paper we discuss three
techniques to make the exokernel design safe and ecient: (1) code inspection, (2) inlined cross-
domain calls, and (3) type-safe languages.
    The contributions of this paper are fourfold. First, we propose a new operating system organiza-
tion that allows applications to control the hardware directly and allows applications to \program"
the operating system kernel by downloading safe extensions into the kernel. Second, we have built
                                                 2
a prototype exokernel system, Aegis, which runs on a MIPS R2000/R3000; it is based on an e-
cient, truly minimal kernel: it implements only ve system calls, it supports the entering of another
addressing context from within the kernel in approximately 20 MIPS assembly instructions, and it
re ects all interrupts, exceptions, and traps to the application in approximately 9 MIPS assembly
instructions. Third, we introduce an ecient variant of sandboxing [45] in which only unrestricted
jumps and privileged instructions have to be controlled instead of all indirect stores and loads.
Fourth, we show how portable dynamic runtime code generation can be used in order to improve
the performance of safe user code that is imported into the kernel; we implemented Mogul's packet-
  lter language [35], compared its performance to an ecient byte-code interpreter, and measured
a factor of 10 performance improvement. All four of our contributions are preliminary, as we do
not yet have fully integrated system that supports all of them in a single system.
     The outline of the rest of the paper is as follows. Section 2 discusses the design of a proto-
type exokernel, Aegis. Section 3 discusses our proposal for a secure programmable machine and
the implementation techniques that permit safe customization across the supervisor mode barrier.
Section 4 reports on an implementation of the Aegis system. In Section 5 we brie y discuss related
work and in Section 6 we conclude.

2 The Aegis Exokernel
We have designed a prototype exokernel, Aegis, to test the feasibility of a system that provides
minimal resource allocation, arbitration services, and a programmable interface. In designing Aegis,
we strictly limited the functionality that is embedded and non-customizable. Many of the primitives
supplied by other \minimalistic" kernels are viewed as applications by the exokernel. For example,
the Aegis kernel does not include page-table management, a le-system, remote procedure call, nor
device drivers.
    To allow ecient checking we have chosen a capability-based approach for our prototype. As
in Amoeba, Aegis capabilities are large random numbers [36]. In a capability-based system specific
resources can be awarded to individual applications. Capabilities enable individual applications
to eciently manipulate the resources they own. The use of probabilistic capabilities also enables
ecient revocation of resource access.
    The design so far has been focused on the minimal set of abstractions that enable applications
to share the available physical hardware. Although it seems dicult to predict how hardware
trends will a ect exokernel design, we do not expect high-level services such as network protocol
implementations or le system management to be exokernel primitives. In the current prototype for
a DECstation, Aegis re ects the following hardware abstractions in its interface: physical memory
pages, the TLB, processors, addressing context identi ers, and interrupt/trap events. In the near
future we will also add direct memory access (DMA) channels and I/O devices.
    Aegis currently supports ve system calls: alloc, dealloc, restrict, yield, and enter. Alloc al-
locates a physical resource (e.g., a time slice, TLB entry, physical memory page, or addressing

                                                 3
context identi er) and returns a capability. Dealloc releases a physical resource. Restrict restricts
a capability. Yield allows another user to use the resource temporarily. Enter is a primitive call to
enter another environment (i.e., an addressing context) through a controlled entry point, called a
gate. As our design progresses, we will only add more systems calls if absolutely needed.
    The entity of accountability in the Aegis kernel is a domain, which consists of one or more
environments and their associated physical resources (e.g., context identi er, physical pages, and
time slices). For example, a database package may be a single domain with multiple environments,
each running a module of the package. The environments are fault isolated from each other. In
addition to the enter mechanism to switch control between environments in different domains,
cooperating environments in the same domain can pass control by just changing their context
identi ers.
    A low-level interface allows applications to set their own policies. Such local policy decisions
may con ict with more effective global policies. For example, two applications may make con icting
policies for a magnetic disk with a single arm. For such a device a global policy is often more effective
than application-specific policies. We are exploring this tradeo between application independence
and global system performance.

3 A Secure Programmable Machine
Aegis provides a programmable virtual machine that permits applications to safely and eciently
manage system resources. Aegis executes in supervisor mode. Our design protects the secure ma-
chine against unsafe environments by using traditional methods: unsafe application code executes
in separate addressing contexts.
    In addition, to permit ecient management of system resources, our design permits controlled
execution of user code in the kernel. This makes the secure machine programmable and enables safe,
ecient customization of the operating system. However, only safe application code may execute
privileged instructions and may execute in the kernel. We are examining several implementation
techniques that permit safe customization across the supervisor mode barrier. These techniques
ensure that safe application code will not execute privileged instructions or access protected data
in uncontrolled ways:
  1. Code Inspection. Code introduced into the secure programmable machine must be free of
     privileged instructions. As shown by Deutsch [12], machine code can be inspected to guard
     against wild loads, stores, and jumps. Execution time can also be controlled by bounding
     loop iteration counts. With suciently stringent restrictions on the application code (or by
     augmenting the application code with checks), it can be safely executed in supervisor mode,
     and primitives of the secure machine that use privileged instructions can be inlined into the
     inspected code.
  2. Inlined cross-domain calls. Code inspection that prohibits indirect loads and stores will
     be too restrictive for many application purposes. Wahbe [45] shows that sandboxing can be
                                                   4
                    OS         Application               Server         OS



                                                                          OS         Driver
                                   Aegis exokernel


                                         Hardware


Figure 1. Software structure of the Aegis system. Each application manages its own physical resources
by containing operating system (OS) code. A small exokernel immediately re ects interrupts, exceptions,
and traps back to the application. Applications can \program" the kernel interface by loading safe pieces of
program into the kernel. (We do not have a le system or a device driver yet.)

      used to restrict the domain of indirect memory operations, but with an overhead of several
      instructions per guarded operation. The motivation behind sandboxing is to simulate address-
      space protection domains when cross-domain calls are expensive. We propose a variant of
      sandboxing that allows user code to execute in supervisor mode, but in a restricted addressing
      context. This scheme eliminates the need to control all indirect loads and stores. Furthermore,
      because Aegis hands out context identi ers and allows cooperating environments to alter the
      context identi er register directly, switching among these environments can be done in only
      a few instructions. Like Aegis they can even safely download foreign application code in their
      environment.
   3. Type-safe language. If applications need to customize the operating system kernel with
      operations that require frequent and intensive manipulation of shared protected data struc-
      tures, then page-granularity protections may not suce. The use of a type-safe language
      and a trusted compiler might enable closer integration of application and kernel code, while
      simultaneously increasing portability. Runtime code generation and other modern compila-
      tion techniques enable the kernel to merge related pieces of code that are downloaded by
      applications.
   We expect each of these techniques to be useful for exokernel extensions, depending on the
tradeo involved.

4 Implementation of the Aegis system
We have implemented a prototype of the Aegis system on a MIPS R2000; Figure 1 depicts its
structure. In addition, we experimented with two customization techniques: one based on safe
                                                     5
languages and runtime code generation, and another based on inlined cross-domain calls.
    The Aegis kernel is an ecient, truly minimal kernel. It does not implement page table manage-
ment, le systems, device drivers, nor remote procedure call; all of these are (or will be) implemented
by applications. It supports only the ve system calls described in Section 2. The implementation of
alloc, dealloc, restrict, and yield are straightforward. Enter allows communication between different
Aegis environments (addressing contexts) by making calls to gates (i.e., entry points) in an another
environment. Each environment supports one gate. A environment calling enter donates the rest
of its time slice to the called environment. Enter implements the bare minimum to allow control
to pass from one environment to another environment. For example, it does not save and restore
registers. Aegis can pass control from one environment to another environment in only 20 MIPS
assembly instructions. A very ecient RPC from client to server can be built if the client trusts
the server to save and restore registers it uses [21]; traditionally RPC systems save and restore at
least all general purpose registers. On the R2000 on which Aegis runs, this costs approximately
64 load and store instructions; as memory speeds are not scaling with processor performance and
processor is increasing, this overhead will become increasingly expensive.
    An Aegis environment is a kernel data structure that consists of an exception handling vector,
a context identi er, and pointers to an application page table, a gate, an epilogue, and a prologue.
The prologue and epilogue code allows applications to save and restore registers under their own
control, and allows them to customize context switches. For example, this allows an application
to implement Bershad's fast uniprocessor synchronization [7] by moving the program counter out
of a critical section and releasing locks on a forced context switch. When Aegis schedules another
environment, it calls the epilogue code of the running environment, installs pointers to the dis-
patch table, page table, and context identi er of the new environment, and then calls the new
environment's prologue code. As even saving and restoring of registers is under application control,
applications can reduce context switching overhead by saving the minimal number of registers; for
example, applications can use their knowledge of active registers to decide which ones to save and
restore.
    Aegis supports context identi ers; address spaces and mappings from virtual to physical are
implemented by applications. This organization allows each application to choose its own page
table layout. For example, an object-oriented system with many small objects may implement
each object in a small address space with a simple page table, while a traditional UNIX system
may implement a multilevel page table hierarchy. In addition, applications have more control over
TLB management, which allows applications to prefetch their own TLB entries, resulting in better
overall performance [5]. The synthetic applications we are currently running all use a very simple
page table layout.
    All interrupts (except for timer interrupts), exceptions, and traps are re ected back through the
environment's dispatch table to the applications in 9 MIPS assembly instructions, allowing each
application to customize its usage of the physical resources. For example, garbage collectors and
distributed shared memory systems can effectively be integrated with the virtual memory systems,

                                                  6
which is also under application control. Thekkath has also recently advocated and exploited the
usage of such inexpensive user-level traps [44]. Aegis can support ecient emulation of multiple
operating system APIs (e.g., BSD4.3, Win32) by tailoring the usage of physical resources to a
specific system and by taking advantage of inexpensive user-level traps.
    Timer interrupts are the only physical resource that is managed by Aegis directly to allow time
sharing of the processor. At a timer interrupt Aegis can also take back physical resources from
badly behaving applications. For example, to revoke physical memory that has been allocated to a
given application, Aegis ushes translations to the allocated physical memory out from the TLB.
Due to space restrictions we restricted our discussion of revocation of physical resources.
    We are investigating multiple ways of safe customization: one using code inspection and inlined
cross-domain calls, and two language-based approaches. We have experimented with an ecient
code inspection scheme that only needs to control jumps and privileged instructions (instead of
jumps and indirect load and stores as in sandboxing [45]) that takes advantage of the architecture
of the MIPS R2000/R3000. The R2000/R3000 can be programmed in such way that user programs
can execute privileged instructions by writing and reading coprocessor 0 [24]. Using this feature,
applications can run controlled privileged instructions in user space while maintaining fault isolation
among different environments. This scheme will work on any architecture that decouples addressing
contexts from the ability to execute privileged instructions.
    We also have experimented with two language-based approaches to safe customization. Using
portable runtime code generation [16] we implemented Mogul's safe packet- lter language and
compared its performance to an ecient byte-code interpreter of the packet lter. We measured
a factor of 10 performance improvement. In addition, we have con gured a small Scheme48 [25]
byte-code interpreter so that it can run inside the Aegis exokernel, allowing us to experiment
with executing safely arbitrary user code in the kernel. We have no results yet on the scheme48
interpreter, but we will report on them in the full paper.

5 Related Work
Many early operating systems papers discussed the need for extensible kernels [18, 23, 29, 30, 46, 47].
Lampson's description of the CAL-TSS [28] and Brinch Hansen's microkernel paper [17] are two
classic rationales. Hydra was the most ambitious system that had the separation of kernel policy
and mechanism as one of its central tenets [47, 32]. Modern revisitations of microkernels have also
argued for kernel extensibility [1, 10, 11, 39, 41, 43]. Anderson and Kiczales et al. also recently
argued for minimalism and customizability [2, 26]. Two important di erences between our work
and previous approaches are that: (1) the xed kernel interface in these systems is a high-level one
(e.g., page-tables are implemented by the kernel) and (2) customization carries a heavy performance
penalty since it is usually accomplished through the addition of servers that interact with the kernel
via IPC.
    To combat this performance penalty, current microkernels allow reintroduction of code into the

                                                  7
kernel: the QNX operating system allows user-level handlers for device I/O [20]; Chorus servers are
loaded into the kernel [41]; Mach 3.0 has migrated some of the AFS cache manager back into the
kernel [38]; the Amoeba le server is usually con gured to run in the kernel [43]; Windows/NT runs
only non-critical services outside of the kernel [11]; Lepreau et. al. has provided a tool to reintroduce
servers into Mach 3.0 [31]. Draves has argued for selecting among several implementations of a
specific kernel abstraction to allow customization [14]. However, none of these customizations
guarantee the safety of the code once introduced.
    Synthesis is an innovative operating system that has inspired some of our work [34]; for example,
the use of runtime code generation. The Aegis system, however, uses a portable runtime code
generation system [16], while the synthesis kernel is written in assembly, and uses ad-hoc runtime
code generation macros to specialize system calls. Furthermore, the Aegis system will use runtime
code generation to eciently execute application kernel extensions.
    Concurrently with our work the SPIN project also investigates adaptable kernels that allow
applications to make policy decisions eciently [6]. The SPIN system encapsulates policies in
spindles that can be dynamically loaded into the kernel. To ensure safety, spindles will be written
in a type-secure language and will be translated by a trusted compiler. In contrast, we anticipate
using a variety of customization techniques that permit safe execution of small pieces of application
code within the exokernel, some of which will allow the kernel interface to be extended using existing
application code. In addition, the exokernel aggressively moves code out of the operating system
kernel into user-space; its kernel interface provides a much low-level interface than microkernels do.
The SPIN project, on the other hand, concentrates more on moving user code into a microkernel.
    Like exokernels the Scout project intends to use modern compiler and language technology
to improve operating systems. Scout mainly intends to use this technology to optimize critical
paths in a communication kernel that is based on their high-performance x-kernel architecture [22].
Exokernels are employ compiler technology both for improving performance and controlling the
execution of user code in the kernel.
    Techniques for certifying the safety of code include inspection and sandboxing. Deutsch showed
how to safely introduce user-written instrumentation code into a running kernel by bounding loads,
stores, jumps and runtime [12]. Making existing binaries safe has been explored by Wahbe [45].
Although this technique will be useful for controlling entry points, we expect that loads and stores
can be constrained more eciently by changing the address context quickly within supervisor mode.
    The use of a type-safe language to allow user applications to augment the operating system
has been explored in a personal workstation environment [40]. Myers argued for using a type safe
language to load application code into the object manager in a persistent object system [37].
    In summary, the Aegis system builds on a rich tradition of operating system and language tech-
nology. Aegis extends it in two key ways: (1) it makes hardware resources directly available to the
application; (2) it award treats application kernel extensions as first class objects by safely incor-
porating them into the operating system. This organization allows aggressive user customization
and subsequently high performance and flexibility.

                                                   8
6 Conclusions
Operating systems must shed the burden of their traditional policy-laden services. We suggest
exokernels as an new minimal operating system design. To minimize the overhead of protection
domain crossings we proposed three customization techniques. We reported on an experimental
exokernel, Aegis. Aegis currently supports ve system calls that allow applications to control the
available physical hardware directly.
    Exokernels allows unprecedented control of the physical hardware resources. We expect that an
exokernel will be an important technology to allow software to scale from small hand-held devices
to powerful general-purpose workstations and high-performance supercomputers.
